_observationFloor:
The portrait is read only down to model Y = -85 mm. Below the collar a portrait shows what the person was wearing, and the chroma guard cannot see it: dividing a near-black pixel by its own sum gives an unstable chroma that lands anywhere, including inside the skin ellipse, which is the price of ignoring brightness so that a shaded neck still reads as skin. A chest dominated by black lace scored 10.2% off-skin by that test.

The height is measured. Adding the term the guard leaves out -- a sample darker than half the first percentile of this person own face luminance is not shaded skin -- and reading the published maps in bands of model height put the whole population under 4.3% down to -85 mm, median 0.0 to 0.1%. Below that the worst subject went 26%, 30%, 42%, 35%: generated-white-girl-01 wore a black lace top, generated-white-boy-01 a cream knit whose ribbing was legible in the sheet, daniel-radcliffe a patterned lapel, rupert-grint and park-eun-bin dark garments. After the floor every band below -85 mm is 0.0 to 0.1% for every subject.

The chest is continued from the median of the lower neck rather than left to the fill. Left to the fill, one stray texel at the collar becomes the whole chest: the first run with the floor put a white block on one shoulder and a dark green one on the other.

This is a decided exclusion. What ships is a face editor; a chest is not in the photograph to be observed.
_fillPull:
The push-pull fill raises each pyramid level by bilinear interpolation, not by repeating each coarse texel into a two-by-two block. Repeating is what a push-pull fill usually does and what made it look like one: at the levels that supply a large hole, one texel became a square hundreds of texels across, and the sheet filled with flat rectangles whose edges were visible on the rendered skin. The forty-eight smoothing passes that follow reach a few texels and could not touch a block that size.

Measured as the largest step inside the reconstructed region, the ninety-nine-point-nine percentile falls by a median of 14.6% and by 28 to 49% on eight subjects, and the share of that region crossed by a sub-quantum step rises from about 88% to about 94%. It changes no observed texel at all: compared texel by texel, the two bakes differ nowhere the photograph decided.

The first measure tried was the mean absolute Laplacian, which said the change was 87.6% worse on all eighteen. That measure rewards plateaus: a block is flat inside and steep only on its boundary, so its mean is small. The picture and the number disagreed and the number was wrong.
_renderCensus:
Both changes were judged by a census of the render rather than by looking at it. Each subject is captured in four states -- bald and dressed, lit and clay -- through the shipped editor. The clay toggle puts one uniform material over the whole scene and changes nothing else, so a lit frame is shading times albedo and its clay frame is shading times a constant, and dividing cancels the light and leaves the albedo as the viewer receives it.

Four numbers: painted, an albedo step the geometry does not explain, as a share of visible skin; asymmetry, the relative left-right difference about the head own axis; holes, skin showing through what the hair encloses; fragments, the share of the hair silhouette in specks. All read on the dressed frame, because that is what ships.

Against the pre-change population: painted median -1.83 points with no subject worse and the least improved at -0.23, asymmetry median -0.060 with none worse, holes and fragments unmoved. That hair is unmoved was predicted before the reading, on the grounds that its worst subjects are a different set entirely.

The instrument needed five corrections of its own before it could be trusted, and the last one mattered most: scaling the albedo by the frame median coupled every reading to everything else in the frame, so when the chest stopped being a white shirt michael-gambon face -- not one texel of which had changed -- read 1.50% to 4.28% worse. A local contrast is invariant to that. The regression was the instrument.
